chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
title: Savoy Ballroom with Roy Eldridge and meeting Dizzy Gillespie
summary: Collins first went to New York with Eldridge, who played opposite Erskine Hawkins, and he noticed Dizzy Gillespie, harmonically different from anyone, jamming with Roy.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Zutty left and we had another drummer by the name of Doc Young -- no, Doc West, Harold West, who was a very fine drummer. You've heard of West. Yeah. So he played with us for quite a while, and then I -- this is the first time I went to New York was with Roy Eldridge. We played the Savoy. At this time Paul Whiteman had acclaimed claimed Roy the world's greatest trumpet player.
And the only trumpet player -- well, we played oppo-

site Erskine Hawkins. He had in the Savoy Ballroom in New York, and Roy would just wipe him out every set, you know, it was just pitiful. Erskine had this band and we'd come on and we were the foot stompers, you know. But the only trumpet player that would come up with -- and jam with Roy was a guy by the name of Dizzy Gillespie. And he played different from anyone.
I noticed this harmonic sense was different -- he was harmonically different from anything I'd ever heard, you know. And he would come and jam on the stand with Roy.

In the Savoy, and I would say well this guy here is something else, you know, because as I say, just the mere fact that he was acclaimed the greatest trumpet player in the world, and Roy was very exciting, you know. But never phased Dizzy at all. He'd barge right in with his innovations and he was innovative, believe me. You know, this is why people talk about who the daddy of bebop and the daddy of this. It was Dizzy Gillespie, nobody else.
Well, Dizzy says that it was an interchange of ideas.
Among him and Bird and Clarke and you.
Yes, but this was before Bird. See, this is before --
